claims.claim: Fire & Blood is a scholarly treatise citing competing fictional primary sources whose conflicts reflect medieval historiography and make Gyldayn unreliable.

Rifkind (Times) called it interminable self-indulgent crap, Dan Jones (Sunday Times) a masterpiece of popular historical fiction, and Chris Lough (Tor.com) the best Song of Ice and Fire book in 18 years.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Fire & Blood (novel)' (secondhand for the paywalled Times pieces and the 404'd Tor.com review)
claims.quote: a masterpiece of popular historical fiction

claims.claim: The chronicle leans on eldritch epochal names such as the Doom of Valyria and the Dance of the Dragons.
The storyline moves briskly across 700 pages, fed by dragons, impaled bodies and betrayals.
Martin creates vivid personalities that leap from the page even when they have no dialogue or on-page appearance, only description.
claims.quote: even when they don't have any dialogue
claims.page: REVIEW: Fire and Blood by George R.R Martin

claims.claim: The history seeds unanswered questions (was Aegon's heir a singer's? was Maegor resurrected?) and often offers its own suggestions as to what happened.
claims.page: REVIEW: Fire and Blood by George R.R Martin

claims.claim: It is a pseudo-history that keeps the salacious details real history downplays, a summary of the good parts in an entertaining, well-formatted style.
claims.quote: A summary of the good parts
claims.page: REVIEW: Fire and Blood by George R.R Martin

claims.feature: reads like real history, not fable
claims.claim: Fire and Blood reads like a real work of history, whereas The Silmarillion reads like a collection of interlinked fables and myths.
claims.quote: more like a real work of history
claims.page: Review of Fire and Blood by George R.R. Martin

claims.claim: Technique-wise the narrative is tight end to end with clear goals and movement, the Martin of old rather than of Feast or Dance.
claims.quote: The narrative is tight, end to end
claims.page: Review of Fire and Blood by George R.R. Martin

claims.claim: The conceit is a history told by a crown-loyal maester who decides what to tell or merely suggest, and who is gossipy about it, adding a layer of interpretation.
claims.source: Jeroen, A Sky of Books and Movies, 30 Nov 2022
claims.quote: he is being gossipy about it too
claims.page: George R.R. Martin – Fire & Blood (2018) Review

claims.claim: Tonally it is unlike The Silmarillion's mythopoetic mode: not written as if it were the King James Bible but as the work of a gossipy historian.
claims.source: Jeroen, A Sky of Books and Movies, 30 Nov 2022
claims.quote: as a work by a gossipy historian
claims.page: George R.R. Martin – Fire & Blood (2018) Review

claims.feature: characters in a couple of lines
claims.claim: Martin sketches loads of colorful, lively characters with just a couple of lines and details.
claims.source: Jeroen, A Sky of Books and Movies, 30 Nov 2022
claims.quote: with just a couple of lines and details
claims.page: George R.R. Martin – Fire & Blood (2018) Review

claims.claim: Battle rosters of lords and knights make the eyes glaze; the impact of battles muddles into a wash of names.
claims.source: Jeroen, A Sky of Books and Movies, 30 Nov 2022
claims.page: George R.R. Martin – Fire & Blood (2018) Review

claims.claim: Many things are only hinted (a queen rumored a witch whose rivals die mysteriously) and never stated outright, so hidden plot threads slip past inattentive readers.
claims.source: Jeroen, A Sky of Books and Movies, 30 Nov 2022
claims.page: George R.R. Martin – Fire & Blood (2018) Review

claims.claim: Gyldayn sometimes places two opposing accounts side by side rather than adjudicating between them.
claims.quote: placed two opposing stories side by side
